subject: Surge playbook proposal and PoC next steps (SLO + warm-pool strategy)
messages:
From: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@acme.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Sarah Lim <sarah.lim@acme.com>
Date: 2026-07-08T16:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Discovery — latency & burst requirements

Ben, thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying points so you can tune a proposed playbook: 

- Business context: we run a chat assistant for customer support. Peak events (product launches, outages) drive short 10–20 minute spikes.
- SLO targets: P99 latency target <= 250ms for non-streaming completions; mean latency target ~120ms. For streaming token-by-token responses we need first-byte latency <= 150ms and steady token streaming < 40ms/token.
- Throughput & concurrency: steady-state ~200 requests/sec (avg), peak bursts up to 600 requests/sec for ~10–20 minutes. Typical concurrency per model instance ~80–150 simultaneous sessions.
- Autoscale expectations: we need capacity to absorb the 600 rps bursts without visible user errors. Target scale-up time: ideally <90s from baseline to peak. If that is not possible, we can accept short queueing behavior but only if queue time <500ms 95% of the time.
- Warm pool: prefer some pre-warmed nodes to reduce cold start costs at launch. We currently have a Reserved-GPU contract on another vendor and are open to a reserved + burst model if it reduces risk.
- Observability: we will need token-level latencies, queue depth metrics, and per-route cost breakdown to evaluate the PoC.

Can you outline what a Redwood surge-playbook would look like given these numbers and call out the tradeoffs (warm pool size vs cost, queueing vs scale aggressiveness)? Also please propose next steps and a timeline for a hands-on PoC so we can sign off with procurement.

Thanks,
Tom
Tom Reynolds
Head of Platform Engineering — Acme Corp
[Attachment: product-launch-triggers.xlsx (xlsx, 45KB)]

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@acme.com>
Cc: Sarah Lim <sarah.lim@acme.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-07-09T09:10:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Discovery — latency & burst requirements

Tom — great summary, very helpful. High-level response and a proposed playbook attached. Key takeaways up-front: 

1) Feasibility: your SLOs are achievable with a hybrid approach: small reserved pool (Dedicated or Dedicated-like capacity) + dynamic warm pool for burst absorption. Streaming-first-byte targets are realistic with pre-warmed weights and continuous batching.

2) Warm pool sizing recommendation: baseline (steady 200 rps) -> provision capacity for steady + 1x typical short burst (so ~400 rps pre-warmed) and allow autoscaler to add the remainder. For your peak 600 rps target, we recommend a warm-pool of 4 pre-warmed nodes (we'll document exact GPU counts in the PoC).

3) Scale-up and queueing tradeoffs: our measurements show aggressive vertical scaling can meet ~60–90s for cold -> warm depending on model size and kernel compilation needs. To keep apparent latency under your 250ms P99, we will: 
  - keep a shallow queueing allowance (<=500ms target) for non-streaming requests to enable batching efficiency,
  - use prefix/KV cache to cut token eval time on resumption, and
  - employ pre-warmed images + prioritized scheduling for critical routes.

4) Streaming: to hit first-byte <=150ms, we'll route streaming requests to dedicated warm endpoints (no batching) with sticky routing during bursts. That costs more but preserves UX.

5) Observability & SLO gates: we will instrument token-level timing, queue depth, scale events, and error budgets; we propose weekly regression alerts tied to your test prompts.

Next steps I propose: 
- Technical deep-dive (60m) with your infra lead (Sarah) + our infra lead (Lauren) — goal: agree exact model footprint and warm-pool sizing (propose Tue 2026-07-13 10:00 PDT).
- Draft PoC plan (3 weeks): load profile tests, failover scenarios, and SLA measurement run. We will provide a test harness and a suggested load schedule.
- Optional: pricing sketch for a 3-month reserved capacity + burst credits to cover warm-pool baseline.

I attached a short playbook outline and will have Lauren follow up with technical timings and an initial set of perf numbers from our internal warm-pool tests.

Best,
Ben Carter
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: surge_playbook_outline.pdf (pdf, 120KB)]

From: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>
Cc: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@acme.com>, Sarah Lim <sarah.lim@acme.com>
Date: 2026-07-10T11:55:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Discovery — latency & burst requirements (technical details)

Ben / Marcus / Tom — following up with specifics from our internal warm-pool runs so Tom can see the numbers that inform the recommendations. Summary bullets: 

- Test setup: 8x A100-equivalent GPUs, model size ~13B, seq len 256, mixed-precision quantization path enabled.
- Observed scale-up: creating a new instance (cold) + kernel warmup for that model path: 70–110s (median ~85s). If we can skip kernel JIT (pre-compiled image) this drops to ~25–40s.
- Warm pool resume time: promoting a pre-warmed instance to traffic takes ~5–8s (network attach + load balancing).
- Steady throughput per instance: ~90–120 rps depending on batching window.
- Queueing behavior: with a 200ms batching window we saw improved throughput by ~20% but added mean queue latency ~80–120ms; P99 queue latency spiked to ~420ms under extreme bursts.

Implications for your SLOs: 
- To keep P99 <=250ms without queuing compromises we recommend pre-warming to cover ~65% of expected peak (so ~4 warm nodes as Ben noted) and sizing autoscaler to add remaining capacity within 90s.
- To satisfy streaming first-byte <=150ms, route streaming to dedicated warm endpoints (no batching).
- If procurement prefers a flat monthly cost, we can size a Dedicated commit that covers the warm pool and use burst credits for additional short-term capacity.

I'll attach the raw CSV of latency vs concurrency so you can eyeball tail behaviors. Marcus, please prepare a PoC load schedule reflecting Acme's launch profile (short 10–20m spikes).

Thanks,
Lauren Bishop
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: warm_pool_latency_test_results.csv]

From: Tom Reynolds <tom.reynolds@acme.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Sarah Lim <sarah.lim@acme.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-07-12T09:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Discovery — latency & burst requirements

Ben / Lauren — this all looks good and actionable. A few quick items from procurement & leadership: 

- Procurement asked for a pricing sketch for a 3-month Dedicated baseline that covers the warm pool (4 nodes) + per-minute burst credits for the 600 rps tail. Can you include an SLA for scaling behavior and an SLA carve-out for streaming endpoints?
- Timeline: we want a 2-week PoC kickoff (agreeing load tests and access), then a 3-week execution window. Can you confirm availability for next Tue 2026-07-13 for the technical deep-dive?
- Success criteria: P99 <=250ms non-streaming; first-byte streaming <=150ms; no user-facing errors during burst tests (error rate <0.01%).

If you can circulate a short statement of work and pricing sketch ahead of the call, procurement will be ready to move quickly.

Appreciate the clear recommendations — Sarah and I will be on the deep-dive.

Tom
Tom Reynolds
Head of Platform Engineering — Acme Corp
